units.unit: Needs a definition of subdivided units and their living conditions
Needs evidence on what rent control does to tenants and landlords
D1 gives the definition and background of SDUs
D3 is a tenant's own account showing what living there is like
SDU tenants pay a premium per square foot
SDU tenants are mostly people stuck waiting for public housing
Mr Chan is split: a cap would save him money but he fears landlords would empty units
Mr Chan says the waiting list matters more than rent
A tighter cap alone might not help much
Wants sources arguing against tighter controls or showing effects
D6 should explain in theory what a cap does to supply
D7 is a real Berlin example to test Mr Chan's fear
D6 says hard caps on initial rent cut supply (elasticity 0.31 to 0.48)
The 2021 HK law only limits increases and has small effects
A 15 percent cut would give incumbents about 900 dollars a month but block 3,000 to 4,000 households a year from entering
Berlin listings dropped and rents jumped after the law fell
This backs up Mr Chan's fear
The NGO report agrees with Mr Chan, who cared more about the waiting list than rent
The real problem is too few places, and a cap only changes the price
The more urgent gap is the data
Need to see if SDU stock really stayed stable after the 2021 law, as D6p2 claims
The source would need to show SDU stock and rents over time
D2 is the data on stock and rents to check D6's claim
D5 is the landlord view
D11 is the NGO survey of tenants that the assistant mentioned
Stock kept growing after the 2021 ordinance, which fits D6's point that limits on increases do not shrink supply
SDU rent burden still got worse, so the ordinance did not fix affordability
The landlord claim about exit has no data behind it, so treat it as a warning, not proof
D11 says tenants want tenure security and a faster offer
Position: do not impose a hard initial-rent cap, but tighten narrowly with tenure security and a light band on initial rents
A light band on initial rents is still a cap on levels and could contract supply if it binds
The band only works if set loose enough not to bind much, which is why D11 says light
The sources give no number for the band
D6p4 shows the risk grows with a 15 percent cut
Picks option 1, claim, evidence, objection, reply, to defend against the landlord and supply objection
Mr Chan said he would accept any rent to leave if the queue were shorter
Wants to know if anything in the archive shows the waiting list being fixed
Claim: Hong Kong should not set a hard cap on initial SDU rents but tighten narrowly with tenure security and at most a loose band, because hard caps shrink supply and hurt entrants
The landlord objection comes first, then the reply
Needs a source showing whether the queue changed; if none, will state that as a limit of the evidence
D10 is a draft not for circulation, so will not use it
D11p2 says enforcement capacity is better spent on inspections of fire and ventilation than on policing rents
Wants a source giving the best case for tightening rent control to answer it fairly
The best case for tightening is D2p2: rent burden rose from 31 to 34 percent even under the ordinance
The burden rose while stock also grew, so the cost fell on rent, not availability
A hard cap risks trading price for availability for the poorest entrants (D6p4)
D1p3 says the ordinance excluded SDUs with co-living services from key provisions
Tightening could mean closing that co-living exclusion gap rather than capping rents
Landlords say a hard cap is confiscatory and they will exit (D5p1, D5p2)
Partly agrees because D6 finds supply does fall under hard caps
They have no data on their margins and their cost figures come from a self-reported survey with a 34 percent response rate (D5p3)
D2p1 shows no exit under the softer 2021 rules
Treats exit as a real risk for a hard cap, not a proven fact, which is why only a narrow tightening is supported
Wants to know what in the archive shows whether rent burden rose because of weak controls or something else; if nothing, will say it is unclear
